the metabolic and nutritional ecology of a bivalve molluscan species which, in common with many others in the intertidal, is subject to pronounced seasonal fluctuations in food availability and in environmental conditions.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
M. edulis exhibits a metabolic strategy in which energy reserves accumulated during somatic growth are utilized to buffer metabolic demands during periods of low environmental productivity.
the mussel M. edulis is an organism which, in common with many others, exhibits a high degree of phenotypic plasticity in its physiological response to environmental conditions.

, in this species at least, metabolic demands are not only met from a range of different sources, but that these sources are themselves subject to a degree of endogenous regulation which may be adaptive in a species which experiences pronounced seasonal changes in food availability and in which feeding and associated activities may account for a significant proportion of the total energy budget.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
M. edulis is an opportunistic feeder that is capable of exploiting a wide range of nutritional resources, but that it is not an immediate optimiser of its feeding behaviour.
, in the mussel, the metabolic costs of feeding are not negligible, that they are not necessarily minimized, and that they may be endogenously controlled in an adaptive fashion.

M. edulis is an opportunistic species, capable of exploiting a wide variety of food types, which is able to maintain a constant level of metabolic activity by adjusting its feeding rate and the utilization of its energy reserves in a flexible manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the metabolic demands of M. edulis are much higher than previously reported.
the metabolic costs associated with feeding in marine invertebrates are substantial and may be as high as 38% of standard metabolic rates.
the energy budget of a mussel can be influenced by the availability of food, the availability of oxygen in the water and the temperature.
